The `uptime` command printed that the system has been running for 21 days, 14 hours, and 44 minutes, that there are currently 2 users logged in, and that the load averages over the past 1, 5, and 15 minutes are 9.93, 12.36, and 15.06 respectively. Load average is a measure of how many processes are either running on the CPU or waiting in the run queue (uninterruptible sleep is sometimes counted too, depending on the system), averaged over those three time windows, so the three numbers tell a short, medium, and longer-term story. Here the 1-minute average is the lowest of the three, while the 15-minute average is the highest, which suggests the load has been climbing for a while and is only now starting to ease — a typical pattern when a big burst of work finishes and the queue gradually drains. On a multi-core box, you compare these numbers to the core count: roughly equal means the system is busy but keeping up, much higher means it is saturated.

For a build server, a sustained high load average is usually a serious problem because builds are exactly the kind of CPU- and I/O-bound, parallelizable work that exposes every weakness in a saturated system. When the15-minute average is15, every compile job is waiting in line behind others, so wall-clock build times balloon and developer feedback loops slow down — instead of a 2-minute incremental build, you might wait 10 or 20 minutes, which quietly kills productivity and tempts people to start more builds in parallel, making the congestion worse. Build servers also tend to do heavy disk I/O (reading source trees, writing object files, running linkers), and on Linux "load average" includes processes in uninterruptible I/O sleep, so a high number can indicate that the storage layer — disk, RAID controller, NFS mount, or cache filesystem like `ccache`/`sccache` sitting on slow media — is the actual bottleneck rather than raw CPU. The right response is to look past the number itself: correlate it with `nproc`, `iostat`, and `top` to see whether you are CPU-bound, I/O-bound, or just running too many concurrent jobs (lowering `-j` parallelism often produces faster overall throughput than fighting the scheduler), and consider whether the hardware is simply under-provisioned for the workload it has been asked to carry.

The `date` command printed `Sat Oct 3 03:45:29 PM EDT 2026`, which means it is currently 3:45 PM (and 29 seconds) in the Eastern Daylight Time zone on Saturday, October 3rd, 2026. The output follows the conventional Unix format: abbreviated day of the week, abbreviated month, day of the month, hour:minute:second with an AM/PM marker, the time zone abbreviation (EDT, which is UTC−4 during daylight saving time), and the four-digit year. This kind of timestamp is one of the most familiar outputs in any Unix-like system and is commonly used in shell scripts, logs, and cron jobs to record when an event happened.

Server clocks drift for several interconnected reasons. The most fundamental is that no real oscillator is perfectly accurate: the quartz crystals used in commodity server hardware oscillate at frequencies that are sensitive to temperature, manufacturing variation, and aging, so each tick of the system clock is slightly longer or shorter than an ideal second, and those tiny errors accumulate over days and weeks into seconds or minutes of skew. Beyond the hardware, virtualization, suspend/resume cycles, and heavy load on the host can introduce pauses or jumps that the kernel's timekeeping subsystem has to correct for, sometimes imperfectly. That is why production systems almost universally run a time synchronization daemon like `chrony`, `ntpd`, or `systemd-timesyncd`, which continually nudges the clock toward authoritative sources (GPS, atomic clocks, or national laboratories) over the network, keeping drift to milliseconds even on hardware that would otherwise wander by seconds per day.
